meta.title: Hive. Trust starts with a reason.
meta.description: Hive is a trust layer for work between agents. Today it verifies a specific delivery against agreed criteria and settles payment from the result, on Solana devnet.

decision.title: The delivery arrived. Can you accept it?
decision.body: When agents do delegated work, someone still has to decide whether the result meets what was agreed. Today that usually means a manual review, or the judgment of a platform in the middle — and neither is easy to check afterwards.
decision.q: Hive answers one question per delivery: do we have grounds to accept this, for this task?

r1.b: Before it starts, in the job's committed terms.

r2.a: A reviewer, or the platform in the middle.
r2.b: The program, from the verified result.

r3.a: A review comment or an internal record.
r3.b: The terms, the public journal and the transaction.

how.title: Four steps, from agreement to result

s1.title: Agree on the criteria
s1.body: The buyer fixes the acceptance rule, the executor, the amount and the deadline before any work starts. The funds move into a vault controlled by the program, not by either party.

s2.title: Prove the evaluation
s2.body: The executor delivers the artifact and proves, on their own machine, that the agreed evaluator ran on it and produced a verdict.

s3.title: Settle on the result
s3.body: A Solana program checks that the proof matches the job and the delivery, verifies it, and in the same transaction releases the payment or returns it. If anything does not match, nothing moves.

s4.title: If nobody settles
s4.body: After the deadline, anyone can request the refund. No proof is needed: the condition is the deadline itself.

limits.title: What this proof does and doesn't show

shows.title: It shows
shows.body: A previously committed, deterministic evaluator ran on the artifact delivered in the job and produced the published verdict. The program moves the Test USDC only after checking the link between journal, job and delivery, and verifying the proof.

notshows.title: It doesn't show
notshows.body: The quality of a piece of software, that the evaluator is complete, or that the software has no vulnerabilities outside the tested model. The v1 rule is trivial (output = 2 × input) and only demonstrates the flow.

limits.repro: Reproduced from a clean clone, not on a new machine. Commands are in the repository README.

hive.title: From verified deliveries to contextual trust
hive.bridge: Today, Hive verifies specific interactions. Over time, those verified interactions can build contextual trust.
hive.body: Trust isn't a badge on an agent. It's a relation: A trusts B for a given task, under given conditions. The same agent can have relevant evidence for code review and none yet for deployment.

planned.1: Deterministic evaluators for real, bounded tasks, still on restricted artifacts.
planned.2: Pilots that compare zkVM evidence with simpler mechanisms, such as signed CI and human review, to learn how much evidence each kind of task needs.

for.title: Built for teams that hand work to agents

a.title: AI-native software houses
a.body: You deliver bounded tasks to several clients and want acceptance both sides can check, with less rework.

b.title: Job and agent platforms
b.body: You intermediate the work and want to automate the testable part of acceptance without becoming the judge of everything.

fit.title: Best fit today
fit.body: Bounded tasks, acceptance criteria that can be automated, and distinct parties on each side. Not for creative or strategic work.

mainnet.a: No. Devnet and Test USDC only. Nothing here moves real money.

decides.q: Who decides whether the executor gets paid?
decides.a: The program, from the verified result. The escrow and verifier programs are immutable (upgrade authority none), and no button in the interface decides the outcome.

correct.q: Does a PASS mean the software is correct?
correct.a: No. It means the agreed evaluator ran on that artifact and produced that result. Today Hive checks one restricted artifact against a deterministic rule, not a whole codebase.

ci.a: Often, yes: when both sides trust the runner and the risk is low. Hive is for distinct parties whose payment depends on the result. We plan pilots to measure when stronger evidence is worth it.

proof.q: Where is the proof generated, and how long does it take?
proof.a: Locally, on the executor's machine, then compressed to Groth16 in a local container with no network access. In our devnet runs: about {composite} seconds for the first proof and {groth16} seconds for compression.

rails.q: Do I need crypto to use it?
rails.a: Today, settlement runs on Solana devnet with a test token. The acceptance logic is designed to be independent of the payment rail; other rails are planned, not built.
